To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

germline TP533 mutations result into a massive and global impairment of p53 DNA-binding and transcriptional response, and that dominant-negative missence mutations are the most severe and clinically relevant.

TP53 mutation carrier lymphocytes exhibit a constitutive p53 transcriptional defect and that this defect is more pronounced with dominant-negative TP53 mutations, which are the most clinically aggressive.
the clinical severity in TP53 germline mutation carriers depends on the nature of the mutation and is explained by a constitutive defect in p53 transcriptional function.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of new biomarkers of the clinical severity of germline mutations in cancer susceptibility genes.
the study of TP53 mutations, which are associated with the Li-Fraumenis syndrome (LFS), a hereditary cancer syndrome.
the study of the molecular mechanisms underlying cancer predisposition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the severity of LFS is explained by the severity of p53 DNA-binding defect.
LFS is not a 'p53 deficiency syndrome' but a 'p53 dysfunction syndrome'.
the clinical severity and penetrance of TP53 germline mutations are directly related to their effect on p53 DNA binding.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
LFS is a disease with a very high genetic penetrance, but a very low phenotypic penetrance.

TP53 dominant-negative mutations, which are associated with the most severe clinical phenotype, result into a constitutively defective p53 DNA binding, whereas the other TP53 mutations result in a more moderate defect.
LFS patients with dominant negative missense mutations of TP53 have a severe clinical phenotype because of a massive and global defect of p53 transcriptional activity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ChIP-Seq is a powerful tool to study the impact of germline p53 mutations in LFS and to understand the molecular mechanisms underlying LFS clinical heterogeneity.
the p53 transcription response to DNA damage is a key determinant of LFS clinical severity.

the p53 functional assays we developed in our lab can be used in clinical practice to identify TP53 dominant-negative mutations, which are the most frequent and most clinically severe germline mutations in LFS.
